 West Asia conflict drives Reliance’s oil-to-chemicals earnings to a record high; opportunities for Indian chemical sector 
 Reliance’s oil-to-chemicals business just had a blockbuster quarter, with earnings hitting an all-time high as Middle East disruptions tightened fuel markets. Higher crude and product prices helped revenue surge, even though freight, premiums and other costs kept a lid on the upside.Why this matters: If you track energy stocks, this is a reminder that geopolitical shocks can work in a refiner’s favour. Reliance said refining margins jumped sharply, crude runs hit records, and its broader quarterly revenue and EBITDA also climbed.Impact on Indian Chemical Sector: Rising global crude and petrochemical prices are creating opportunities for Indian chemical manufacturers through improved realisations and inventory gains. Reliance’s record O2C earnings highlight the potential benefits of stronger downstream margins. However, higher feedstock, energy and freight costs could squeeze margins for import-dependent specialty chemical companies, creating an uneven sectoral impact. ETChemicals

 Reliance Industries ’ latest quarter underlines a familiar truth about refining: when crude supply chains tighten, margins can widen quickly. In the September quarter, the conglomerate’s oil-to-chemicals business posted its highest-ever earnings , helped by a surge in global fuel cracks after conflict-related disruptions in the Middle East squeezed availability across key markets. Record quarter for the core energy engine The oil-to-chemicals, or O2C, division reported revenue of ₹2.32 lakh crore in the second quarter of FY27, up 44.2 per cent from a year earlier, driven largely by higher energy prices. Reliance said crude oil prices were 40.6 per cent higher than a year ago, while transportation fuel prices rose between 50 per cent and 78 per cent. Downstream chemical product prices also moved up, with most categories increasing 25 per cent to 35 per cent, according to the company’s quarterly results statement. That pricing backdrop translated into a sharp jump in profitability. O2C earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation climbed 67.9 per cent to a record ₹25,203 crore, reflecting unusually strong transportation fuel cracks and better downstream chemical spreads. For a business that sits at the centre of Reliance’s industrial portfolio, the quarter was a reminder that global energy shocks can still swing earnings materially even for a company with scale and integrated operations. Why margins improved so sharply Reliance said the biggest support came from fuel cracks, the gap between the market price of refined products and the cost of crude used to make them. Those cracks rose three to 3.7 times from a year earlier and touched historic highs during the quarter. Singapore-region gasoline, diesel and jet fuel cracks also strengthened significantly year on year, the company said, as supply disruptions tightened product balances. The company linked the market squeeze to several factors at once. Supplies through the Strait of Hormuz were disrupted, refinery outages hit parts of the Middle East and Russia, and inventories were already lower than usual. Together, those conditions reduced available fuel in international markets and pushed up product prices faster than crude in several trading hubs. Higher prices did not mean a free pass Even with stronger realisations, the benefit to earnings was not a simple one-to-one gain. Reliance said higher crude premiums, elevated freight costs, special additional excise duty, and under-recoveries in its domestic fuel retail business all weighed on the division’s performance. In other words, the same market conditions that lifted sales values also made procurement and logistics more expensive. The company’s comments suggest the quarter was a classic case of offsetting forces within the energy chain. Higher crude and product prices boosted revenue, but they also raised input costs and transport charges. That is why the rise in revenue outpaced the improvement in earnings, even though the operating environment was favourable for refiners overall. How Reliance kept refineries running To manage the disruption, Reliance altered crude sourcing patterns and tapped supplies from multiple geographies to keep refinery throughput steady. The company said it achieved record crude runs by buying from the affected region as well as from Latin America , North America and the Mediterranean . This diversification helped cushion the impact of wider Arab Gulf crude differentials and a 15 to 20-fold jump in freight rates, according to the results statement. That sourcing flexibility has become more important as geopolitical risk increasingly affects shipping lanes, insurance costs and crude differentials. For a complex refiner such as Reliance, the ability to switch barrels across regions can determine whether disruptions remain manageable or become a direct hit to utilisation and margins. The quarter also shows how integrated players can use trading and logistics agility to defend operations when supply routes become volatile. What the O2C surge meant for the group The stronger O2C performance fed directly into Reliance’s consolidated numbers. Group revenue rose 27.8 per cent year on year to a record ₹3.62 lakh crore, while consolidated EBITDA increased 23.9 per cent to ₹62,409 crore. The company attributed much of the rise in revenue to sharply higher crude and product prices rather than to volume growth alone. For investors, the results reinforce two takeaways. First, Reliance remains highly exposed to global energy cycles despite its broader diversification across telecom, retail and new energy. Second, geopolitical disruptions can be a double-edged sword: they may lift refinery earnings, but they also raise procurement, freight and working-capital pressures across the value chain. That balance is likely to matter in the coming quarters if Middle East tensions continue to shape trade flows and pricing. For now, the September quarter has delivered Reliance an unusually strong earnings boost from its refining and chemicals business, even as the same conflict kept a lid on how much of the price surge could be converted into pure profit.
